rows: Type HT (2100° F) or lined masonry

steps: Unpack & inspect
Inspect the stove and parts for shipping damage. Remove the packaging in the flue collar and above the baffle before installing the chimney.

Pack list: the Model 8640 woodstove and the owner's manual. Report damaged or missing parts to the Hearthstone dealer right away.

The label is attached by a cable to the bottom of the stove; don't damage it when lifting. After final positioning, store it in the holding clip on the bottom shield.
Choose the location
Freestanding room heater only, never in a factory-built fireplace. Prefer a main living area; confirm clearances to walls, floor, ceiling and chimney chase before connecting.
Floor protection
Non-combustible protector under and beyond the stove: min. 33in x 31-1/2in (US) or 43in x 40in (Canada). No insulated hearth pad and no R-value requirement.
Clearances to combustibles
Position to the Figure 4 table for the connector (single or double wall) and shield in use. Alcove: min. width 51.25", min. ceiling 56". Trim and mantel per Figure 6 (p. 13).
Wall pass-through
Through a combustible wall, build the thimble or pass-through to one of methods A–D; the installation must conform to NFPA 211 or CAN/CSA-B365.

• A. Min. 3.5in thick brick masonry framed into the wall, min. 12in of brick from clay liner to combustibles; fire clay liner from the outer brick surface to, not beyond, the inner surface of the flue liner, cemented in place.
  • B. Solid-insulated, listed factory-built chimney length, same inside diameter as the connector, 1in or more of insulation, min. 9in air space to combustibles.
  • C. Sheet steel connector, min. 24 gauge, with a ventilated thimble (min. 24 gauge, two 1in air channels), separated from combustibles by min. 6in of glass fiber insulation; opening covered, thimble supported with min. 24 gauge sheet steel.
  • D. Solid insulated, listed factory-built chimney length with an inside diameter 2in larger than the connector, 1in or more of insulation, as a pass-through for a min. 24 gauge single wall connector; min. 2in air space to combustibles; min. 12in long; connector spaced 1in by sheet steel support plates at both ends; fasteners must not penetrate the flue liner.
Outside air (if used)
Optional kit 96-53400 to a min. 3" duct, terminated no higher than the stove's air intake, screened and hooded. In Canada add a damper allowing 100% closure and fasten the stove to the floor.
Install the chimney connector

6" 24 or 25 MSG blued steel, or listed double wall. Crimped ends toward the stove; three #10 x 1/2" sheet metal screws at every joint, including the flue collar. Horizontal runs rise at least 1/4" per foot.

• Keep it as short and straight as possible, with the stove as close to the chimney as practical; extra length and elbows add draft resistance and creosote.
  • Never through a floor, ceiling, attic or roof space, closet or similar concealed space. No aluminum or galvanized pipe.
  • Wall thimble required through a combustible wall; wall pass-through (chimney support package) when connecting through a wall or ceiling to a prefabricated chimney.
  • A cleanout tee is recommended where possible.
Connect to the chimney

Listed Type HT (2100° F) chimney per UL 103 or ULC S629, or code-approved masonry with a flue liner. 6" ID flue for new installs; existing 8" with a reducer. Never a shared flue. Check the draft at installation.

Note: p. 15 gives the required draft as 0.06" to 0.1" WC; p. 16 gives -0.06" to -0.15" water column. For drafts above 0.1" WC, install a stovepipe damper (p. 15).
  • Chimney at least 3 feet (0.9 m) above the roof opening and at least 2 feet (0.6 m) higher than any part of the roof within 10 feet (3 m).
  • Prefabricated chimney: buy the wall pass-through or ceiling support, tee, fire-stops, insulation shield, roof flashing and cap from the same maker, and follow its instructions.
  • Masonry: have a professional inspect it first and complete repairs; the clean-out door must seal tightly.
Mobile home (if applicable)

Install per 24 CFR Part 3280 (HUD): outside air kit required, stove permanently fastened to the floor with the shipping clips, and a listed mobile home chimney & connector kit. Never in a sleeping room.

The kit (US/UL103 or CAN/ULC-S629) must include a stainless spark arrester cap, storm collar, adjustable vented flashing 0/12 – 6/12, two 24" chimney pipes, and a 24" support box with built-in starter section and trim.

  • Maintain the structural integrity of the walls, floor, ceiling and roof, and an effective vapor barrier where the chimney penetrates.
  • Remove the chimney when transporting the mobile home.
First fires
Run break-in fires first: small, warm-not-hot fires to season the soapstone and cure the furnace cement. Inspect (and clean if needed) the stovepipe and chimney once break-in is complete.

panels.title: Stove smokes
items: Operating technique → open the air control fully a minute before opening the door, and the bypass first
Cold chimney or reverse draft → preheat the chimney; briefly open a window in the room
Blocked chimney → check chimney and stovepipe for blockage or creosote
Chimney oversized, undersized or too short → reline, fit a draft inducer or replace, or lengthen
Air leaks into the chimney → seal connections and openings; check clean-out doors
Bypass not closed, or catalysts not working → close the bypass in the active range; inspect, brush or replace catalysts

panels.title: Back-puffing or gas explosions
items: Operating technique → air control fully open a minute before opening the door and for a few minutes after reloading; bypass open first
Extra low burn rate → burn at a higher rate
Chimney down-draft → install a chimney cap
Excessive ash build-up → empty ashes more often; avoid poor-quality or green wood

panels.title: Uncontrolled or short burn
items: Unsealed or open door, or air leaking at the glass gasket → close the door tightly; replace gaskets
Excessive draft → check the installation, run at low burn; correct draft over 0.1 wc with stovepipe damper(s)
Extra long or oversized chimney → shorten or reline; stovepipe damper(s)
High winds or hilltop location → install a chimney cap

panels.title: Catalyst trouble
items: Fly ash on catalysts → brush the cold combustor with a soft-bristled brush or vacuum lightly; follow the light-off procedure
Char and fly ash from cardboard, gift wrap or garbage → burn only dry, seasoned wood
Plugging from wet or pitchy wood, or no light-off with the bypass closed → burn dry wood; burn hot with the bypass open until well in range, then run high for one hour
Warping or bowing → too hot for too long; lower the air setting to keep catalysts in range

light.title: Starting a fire
light.html:
Build the fire right on the firebox floor; don't use a grate. For an everyday fire:

  1. Open the bypass handle. Open the front door and put five or six double sheets of tightly twisted newspaper in the center of the firebox.
  2. Stand about 10 pieces of kindling (1/2" in diameter, 10" to 16" long) over the paper like a tee-pee.
  3. Open the primary air control fully: pull the lever all the way out.
  4. Light the paper under the kindling. Leave the door slightly open for a moment, until the kindling burns and the draft starts to pull. Then close the door.
  5. Once the kindling is burning, add logs, small ones first. Keep them away from the glass.
  6. When the fire is burning well and the catalyst thermometer reads active, close the bypass handle.
  7. Let it run on a high setting for about 20 minutes so the catalyst stays active. Then set the burn rate with the air control.
Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen up a fire. Keep them well away from the stove.
It's hot while it runs. Keep children, pets, clothing and furniture away, and keep the door closed while it's in use. A new stove, or the first fire of the season, gets the gentler break-in fire instead.

bypass.title: The bypass & catalyst thermometer
bypass.html:
Your stove burns up its smoke in a catalytic combustor, which starts working at around 500 °F. The bypass handle sends smoke around the catalyst (open) or through it (closed).

Handle points to the frontBypass open
Handle points to the rearBypass closed

Open the bypass

  • When you start a fire, until the catalyst heats up.
  • Every time, before you open the front door to load wood.

Read the thermometer

InactiveKeep the bypass open until the stove heats up
ActiveClose the bypass and leave it closed
Too HotKeep the door closed, move the air control all the way in, and let it cool back to Active

The stove typically runs between 800 °F and 1300 °F. Once the catalyst is active, the burning smoke keeps it hot as long as there's wood in the stove.

The catalyst needs a look at least three times each heating season. With the stove cool, brush fly ash and soot off its face with a soft-bristled brush; the maintenance section (p. 25) shows how to reach it.

air.title: Air control, burn rates & reloading
air.html:
The primary air control lever sits under the ash lip. Pull it out for more air and more heat; push it in for a slower burn. It never closes completely.

LowLever all the way in
Medium-lowFrom low, pull forward a little less than 1/4"
Medium-highFrom low, pull forward a little less than 3/8"
HighLever all the way out

Medium-low is the typical setting and the better choice when you leave the stove alone. Long stretches on low can build creosote. The minimum setting is fixed at the factory; altering it is against federal regulations.

Reloading without smoke

  1. Open the bypass handle first.
  2. Open the door just a crack, pause, then open it fully.
  3. Load onto a bed of hot, red coals. A small valley in the coals behind the lower air opening helps it relight.
  4. If the fire had burned down to coals, run it at medium to high for about 10 minutes so the catalyst reaches about 600 °F, then close the bypass.
Note: for the burn after reloading, p. 23 gives about 10 minutes at a medium to high rate (for a cool fire or one burned down to coals); p. 29 gives 15 to 20 minutes with the air control fully open, so less creosote builds up in the chimney.

breakin.title: Breaking in your stove
breakin.html:
Soapstone has to be seasoned: its natural moisture must be driven out slowly, and the furnace cement must cure. Over-firing a new stove can crack the soapstone.

  1. Open the bypass handle. Put five or six double sheets of tightly twisted newspaper in the center of the firebox, with about ten pieces of kindling (1/2" in diameter, 10" to 16" long) crisscrossed over them.
  2. Open the primary air control fully.
  3. Light the paper. Leave the door slightly open until the kindling burns and the draft pulls, then close it.
  4. Keep a steady, low fire. The stove should get warm but not hot to the touch. Add a few small chunks of wood at most.
  5. Once it's warm, push the air control fully in, let the fire die out and let the stove return to room temperature.
Steam, boiling moisture or hissing means the soapstone is too hot.

Build the first fire of every season the same way.

Smoke and smells at first are normal

The paints and oils give off smoke and fumes, usually for 10 to 20 minutes; open a few windows if needed. These cool fires can dirty the glass (a good hot fire cleans it) and build creosote fast, so have the stovepipe and chimney checked after break-in. Over time the soapstone may change color and show small surface fractures. That doesn't affect how it works.

wood.title: Choosing firewood
wood.html:
Burn only natural firewood (cordwood). The stove isn't designed for any other fuel.

Never burn

  • Coal, charcoal, pellets, artificial or wax logs, or compressed wood
  • Garbage or trash, paper products (including colored, glossy or gift wrap paper), cardboard, plywood or particleboard, driftwood (including salt water driftwood) or other previously salt-water saturated materials, unseasoned (green or wet) wood, or painted, treated, pressure-treated or kiln-dried wood
  • Lawn clippings, materials containing rubber (including tires), materials containing plastic, waste petroleum products, paints or paint thinners, solvents, asphalt products, materials containing asbestos, construction or demolition debris, railroad ties, manure or animal remains
  • Flammable fluids, or highly volatile fuels or combustibles

Burning these can release toxic fumes, or make the stove ineffective and cause smoke. Charcoal, pellets, coal, artificial logs or any other material used as fuel are not safe. Fire starters made from paper, cardboard, sawdust, wax or similar substances are fine for starting a fire.

Wood preservatives, metal foils, plastic, sulphur or oil can also damage the catalyst.

Burning any fuel other than wood could generate dangerous levels of carbon monoxide in the living space. Using an unauthorized fuel such as coal could produce high levels of carbon dioxide in the living space; at high levels, carbon dioxide could result in personal injury or death.

Dry wood burns best

Hardwoods burn longer and leave better coals; softwoods burn hotter and faster. The manual's chart ranks species by heat content: hickory and white oak rank high, sugar maple and red oak medium high, aspen and white cedar low.

Season green wood before you burn it: split it, stack it and let it air dry for a year. Seasoned firewood is usually at or near 20% moisture, which a hand-held moisture meter can check.

Stack wood on skids or blocks and cover only the top; tarps over the sides trap moisture. Don't store firewood within the stove's clearances, and never load ice-crusted wood into a burning stove.

ash.title: Removing and storing ashes
ash.html:
Empty the ashes at the end of every week, or sooner if the firebox is full. You can leave a thin layer in the firebox if you like.

  1. Let the fire die down or go out completely.
  2. Push large live coals to the side and remove only the finer ash with a fireplace shovel.
  3. Put the ashes straight into a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Nothing else goes in it, and don't pour water in.
  4. Put the lid on. Set the container on a noncombustible floor or on the ground outside, well away from anything that burns, liquid fuels and vehicles.
  5. Keep the ashes in the closed container until every coal is cool.
Coals in ashes can stay hot for several days. Never put ashes in wooden or plastic containers, paper or plastic bags, or a trash can with other trash. Never set the container on a combustible surface or vinyl flooring.

Don't let ashes build up around the front door opening. They can spill out, or pack into the gasket channel so the door no longer seals.

glass.title: Glass & door gasket
glass.html:
Clean the glass only when the fire is out and the glass is cool.

  1. Inside: dip a damp paper towel in gray ash and rub the glass in circles.
  2. Finish with window cleaner or a commercial stove-glass cleaner, inside and out.
  3. Wipe off with a soft cloth or black-and-white newsprint.
Note: on the cleaner, p. 30 suggests window cleaner or a commercial stove-glass cleaner, then says to use only a cleaner made specifically for woodstoves.

Never use a razor blade, steel wool or anything abrasive; scratches weaken the glass. Glass that always stays dirty means the fire runs too cool or the wood is wet.

Don't run the stove with broken glass, and don't slam the door. Replacement glass is kit 96-58405 from your dealer.

Note: p. 28 says only a qualified service person should replace the glass; p. 30 says the glass kit includes instructions and everything needed for the repair, and to wear work gloves and safety glasses if you replace it yourself.

Door gasket

Every other month, try the dollar-bill test: with the stove cool, shut the door on a dollar bill. If it pulls out with no resistance, adjust the latch or replace the gasket. Replace the gasket every two to three seasons, or when it's worn or loose.

chimney.title: Creosote & chimney fires
chimney.html:
When wood burns slowly and cool, tar and vapors condense in the chimney as creosote. If it ignites, it burns extremely hot and can damage the chimney or even destroy the house.

  • Check daily for creosote build-up until experience shows how often you need to clean to be safe.
  • Inspect the chimney connector and chimney at least once every two months in the heating season, and at least monthly if build-up is forming.
  • Check at the stove connection and at the chimney top, where it's coolest.
  • Remove creosote thicker than 1/4". A certified chimney sweep is recommended.
  • Have the whole system professionally inspected before each heating season.
  • Prevent it: run with the air control fully open for 35 to 45 minutes every day, and burn dry wood.
Chimney fire? If it's threatening, leave and call the fire department. Otherwise close the primary air control, the stovepipe damper (if there is one) and the bypass, and keep the front door closed. Never throw water on the stove, stovepipe or chimney. Afterward, let the fire die out and inspect the stove, stovepipe and chimney for damage before using it again (p. 6).

overfire.title: Signs of over-firing
overfire.html:
Never over-fire your stove. Over-firing means running the stove hotter than a normal high burn. It damages the stove, and any sign of it voids your warranty.

Warning signs

  • Warped parts
  • Short burn times
  • A roaring sound in the stove or stovepipe
  • Discolored stovepipe

Common causes

  • Too much draft: your dealer can take a draft reading; a stovepipe damper may be needed.
  • The wrong fuel: coal, kiln-dried lumber, wax logs, compressed wood or anything other than natural cordwood.
  • Operator error: worn or compressed gaskets, or burning with a door open.
If you think it's over-firing, stop using the stove and call your dealer right away.

If the catalyst thermometer reads Too Hot, keep the door closed, move the air control all the way in and let it cool back to Active (p. 20).

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Hearthstone's limited warranty covers defects in material or workmanship for the original purchaser, when an authorized Hearthstone dealer installed the stove. It can't be transferred and starts on the original invoice date. "Limited Lifetime" means 10 years.

Stone; cast iron not listed elsewhereLimited Lifetime
Door handles and latches; steel components and firebox5 years
Enamel finish, accessories, glass, components not listed elsewhere1 year

Rows marked for only some fuel types are in the grid on p. 37.

The catalysts

Their maker, Applied Ceramics, warrants them directly. One that stops working within two years is replaced free if you send the bill of sale and the old catalyst, and it wasn't abused or run on the wrong fuel. After that, prorated prices run from $130.00 in year 3 to $160.00 in year 6.

Note: on the free-replacement period, the catalyst warranty says two (2) years, then says each defective catalyst returned "during the three year period" gets one replacement (p. 36).

Not covered

  • Over-firing, or fuels the manual doesn't specify
  • Not installing, running or maintaining it as the manual says
  • Normal wear on parts like gaskets, baffles, paint and glass

For a claim, contact your original Hearthstone dealer.

specOutput.title: Heat output & firebox
specOutput.html:
Maximum heat output40,000 BTUs per hour of cordwood
Heated areaUp to 1,400 square feet
Firebox capacity1.32 cubic feet
Maximum log lengthUp to 16" (40.6cm)
Burn timeUp to 16+ hrs. (Heat Life™: up to 20 hours)
Maker's website: HeatLife: 16 Hours of heat.

Output is based on independent laboratory test results. Insulation, windows, floor plan, stove placement and fuel quality can reduce the area heated. Wood per cubic foot of firebox varies from 10 to 25 lbs. with species, moisture content and packing density.

specEmis.title: Emissions & efficiency
specEmis.html:
Particulate emissions1.07 g/hr
Weighted average efficiency79% (HHV)
Output under EPA test conditions14,000 to 24,000 Btu

Certified to the U.S. EPA 2020 particulate emissions standard using crib wood (EPA Method 28R, 40 CFR Part 60). Efficiency is weighted across the 4 burn rate categories per EPA Method 28R and CSA B415-10. The rating page prints the emission rate as "1.07 gr/hr."; the specifications (p. 7) print "1.07 g/hr."

CO emissions by burn level

Category 1 (low)40.7 g/hr
Category 2 (med. low)16.3 g/hr
Category 3 (med. high)8.6 g/hr
Category 460.1 g/hr

The manufacturer-set minimum low burn rate must not be altered (federal regulations).

specDims.html:

Width23 1/4" (59.1cm)

The dimension drawing is Figure 1 on this page. The label hangs on a cable under the stove: protect it when lifting, and after final positioning store it in the holding clip on the bottom shield (p. 8).

specChimney.title: Connector & chimney
specChimney.html:
Connector6" (152 mm) diameter, 24 MSG or 25 MSG blued steel
New installations6" (152 mm) inside diameter flue
Existing flue8" (203 mm) diameter, with a reducer
Masonry6" round or 8" x 8" square flue

Connect to a listed Type HT (2100° F) chimney per UL 103 or ULC S629, or to a code-approved masonry chimney with a flue liner. The chimney should not be smaller than the flue collar or more than three times its cross-sectional area; an oversized flue builds creosote.

  • No aluminum or galvanized pipe; don't use stovepipe as a chimney.
  • Double wall (air-insulated) connector reduces clearances: Simpson Dura Vent DVL and Metalbestos DS recommended; Security, GSW and Ameritec also acceptable.
  • Never connect to a flue serving another appliance, or to any air distribution duct or system.
  • Masonry liner: tile with min. 5/8" wall and at least 1" air space, or UL listed 6" stainless steel, insulated or wrapped.

specDraft.title: Draft & chimney height
specDraft.html:
Note: p. 15 gives the required draft as 0.06" to 0.1" WC; p. 16 gives -0.06" to -0.15" water column.

For drafts above 0.1" WC, install a stovepipe damper (p. 15; repeated on pp. 24 and 32, where some installs need more than one). Check the draft at installation.

Min. height, top of stove16 feet (4.9 m) off the floor, or 13 feet 7 1/4 inches (4.2 m) from the top of the stove
Min. height, rear exit19 feet (5.8m) off the floor, or 16 feet 7 1/4 inches (5.1m) from the top of the stove
Recommended max. height30 feet (9m)
Above the roof openingAt least 3 feet (0.9 m)
Roof within 10 feet (3 m)Chimney at least 2 feet (0.6 m) higher

Interior chimney: at least 2" (51 mm) to combustibles, fire stops where it passes floors and ceilings, insulation at least 2" (51 mm) away. Exterior chimney: at least 1" (25 mm) to combustibles.

specClear.title: Clearances to combustibles
specClear.html:
Wall clearances for parallel, corner and alcove installs are lettered dimensions A–F in the Figure 4 drawing and table on this page, for a single or double wall connector with the rear heat shield or blower kit shield, and for a single wall connector without the rear heat shield. The letters are defined only in the drawing, so read the values there.

Figure 4, single wall connector with blower kit shieldA 14", B 13.75", C 18", D 25.5", E 7", F 17.25"
Figure 4, double wall connector with blower kit shieldA 14", B 9.75", C 14", D 25.5", E 7", F 17.25"
Maker's website: Clearances, with blower kit heat shield: Side 14", Rear 9¾", Corner 7". Install to the clearance diagrams in the manual.
Minimum alcove width (unprotected)51.25" – 131cm
Min. alcove ceiling, single wall connector56" – 142.3cm
Min. alcove ceiling, double wall connector56" – 142.3cm
Furniture, drapes, clothingAt least 36" (0.92 m)
  • Connector clearances: Figure 5, p. 11. For double wall pipe to the ceiling, follow the pipe maker's specifications.
  • Double wall values are specific to Simpson DuraVent DVL and may vary with other brands.
  • Trim and mantel clearances are a drawing only (Figure 6, p. 13).
  • NFPA 211-approved wall protection can reduce clearances, with approval of the local authority.
  • Blower kit: use kit #96-57400.

specFloor.title: Floor protection
specFloor.html:
US minimum33in x 31-1/2in
Canada minimum43in x 40in
Insulated hearth padNot required

On a combustible floor, a non-combustible floor protector must be under the stove and extend beyond it, for example a hearth with a continuous layer of tile, brick, slate, glass or another non-combustible facing. There is no R-value requirement. The hearth dimensions are drawn in Figure 3 on this page.

LVP or LVT flooring: some begins to warp at 110° Fahrenheit. Check the flooring maker's maximum temperature; additional shielding may be needed.

specAir.title: Outside air
specAir.html:
Outside air kit#96-53400 (optional)
DuctMinimum 3" (76 mm) diameter, supplied by others
Adaptor for 4" ductKit #90-53308

The kit attaches to the underside of the stove; follow its instructions. The IRC doesn't allow the duct to terminate higher than the appliance, and Hearthstone recommends terminating at the same level as, or lower than, the stove's air intake. Place the termination where snow or leaves can't block it, screen it with ¼" x ¼" mesh rodent screen and cover it with a rain/wind proof hood.

  • Canada: install a damper allowing 100% closure, and fasten the stove to the floor with the shipping clips.
  • Mobile homes: an outside air kit is required (p. 18).
  • Consider outside air if the stove doesn't draw steadily, smoke rolls out, other fuel-fired equipment back-drafts, or the house is tightly sealed or has exhaust devices (p. 5).

index_extra.p: What to do if the chimney catches fire
Smoke and fumes from the first fires are normal
Close the bypass once the catalyst is active
Season firewood a year, to near 20% moisture
Check the door seal every other month

conflicts.issue: Required draft is 0.06" to 0.1" WC on p. 15 (damper above 0.1" WC, repeated on pp. 24 and 32) but -0.06" to -0.15" water column on p. 16. Also flagged in step7.
Hot burn after reloading: about 10 minutes at a medium to high firing rate (p. 23) vs 15 to 20 minutes with the primary air control fully open (p. 29).
Glass cleaner: 'window cleaner or commercial stove glass cleaners' vs 'Use a cleaner specifically manufactured for woodstoves only' (both p. 30).
Glass replacement: 'Only a qualified service person should replace the glass panel' (p. 28) vs 'If you replace the glass yourself, wear work gloves and safety glasses' (p. 30).
Catalyst warranty: no-charge replacement if it ceases to function within two (2) years, but the same section says one replacement per defective catalyst 'during the three year period' (p. 36).
